claim: The main-track judging rubric is exactly three criteria, explicitly equally weighted, scored by three independent judges — but a second phase adds undisclosed criteria.
reasoning:
I fetched the cited hackathon page and the official BNB Chain blog post and interrogated both specifically for weighting language.

WHAT SURVIVES SCRUTINY (confirmed against the live page):
1. "Exactly three criteria" — CONFIRMED. The main BNB Chain track lists exactly three criterion headings in order: Functionality, Data Quality, Agent Diversity. Independently corroborated by the official blog: "Submissions are scored against published criteria covering functionality, data quality, and agent diversity."
2. The three verbatim blurbs quoted by the researcher — CONFIRMED, they match the page.
3. "Three independent judges" — CONFIRMED in substance.
4. "A second phase adds undisclosed criteria" — CONFIRMED verbatim, typos and all: "We'all also assess more criterias in the second phase, stay tuned to find out!" The timeline also shows a Phase 2 entry whose content is redacted.
5. "No numeric percentages are published for the main track" — CONFIRMED.

WHAT IS FALSE (the load-bearing error):
"Explicitly equally weighted" is fabricated. I searched the full page for "weight", "weighted", "equally", "equal weight", and "%". The main track carries NO weighting language of any kind — no percentages, no statement of equal weighting, no statement of unequal weighting. The rubric is published unweighted. The researcher inferred equal weighting from the absence of percentages, which is not the same thing, and their own supporting detail contradicts their headline: they concede "No numeric percentages are published for the main track" while asserting the weighting is "explicit." Absence of a stated weighting is not an explicit equal weighting.

Note on where "equal" DOES appear: the word "equal" occurs inside the Agent Diversity blurb ("surfaced with equal depth"), which is about giving the four agent CATEGORIES equal coverage in the product — not about how the three CRITERIA are weighted against each other. This looks like the likely source of the researcher's error: conflating equal depth across agent categories with equal weight across judging criteria.

SECOND, SMALLER ERROR — a truncated quote:
The researcher quotes the judging note as "Three judges, scored independently." The actual sentence on the page is "Three judges, scored independently, then compared." Dropping "then compared" is not cosmetic: it removes the reconciliation step and makes the process look like a pure independent-average, when the page describes independent scoring FOLLOWED BY comparison between judges.

CONTRAST THAT PROVES THE POINT: the same page DOES publish explicit numeric weights, but for a different track. The TermiX Challenge states Value of services 30%, Proven agent advantage 30%, High-stakes categories & track record 20%, Marketplace quality 20%. So BNB Chain publishes weights when it intends to. The main track's silence on weighting is a deliberate contrast, not an implicit 33/33/33.

FALSE LEAD I CHECKED AND DISMISSED: a web-search summary claimed the criteria cover "functionality, data quality, agent diversity, and real-world usage," implying a fourth criterion. I re-fetched the page and specifically asked whether any criterion about usage, traction, or adoption exists. It does not. "Real-world usage" is a search-summarizer artifact, not page text. The three-criteria count stands.

ON THE TOPIC FRAMING (not asserted in the claim, but flagged because the parent may carry it forward): the topic header references "the live ERC-8004/ERC-8183 substrate on BSC." The sources do not support treating that as a live, specified substrate. The blog mentions ERC-8004 only as background ("Agents registered under ERC-8004 already carry an onchain identity and a track record other software can look up," with a claimed "roughly 60% of all registered agents across 26 networks"). ERC-8183 appears only as a BONUS integration under the Altana partner track, alongside x402/B402 — not as a main-track requirement. Critically, NO contract addresses, ABIs, or deployment details appear in either source. Any engineer told there is a "live ERC-8004/ERC-8183 substrate on BSC" they can build against should treat that as unverified until an address is produced.
corrected_claim: The main BNB Chain track rubric is exactly three published criteria — Functionality, Data Quality, and Agent Diversity — with NO published weighting of any kind: no percentages, and no statement that they are equally weighted. The page says "Three judges, scored independently, then compared," and separately warns "We'all also assess more criterias in the second phase, stay tuned to find out!" [sic]. By contrast, the TermiX partner track DOES publish explicit numeric weights (30/30/20/20), which shows the main track's unweighted presentation is deliberate rather than an implicit equal split.
engineering_impact:
Three concrete failure modes if AiKi builds on the false version:

1. MISALLOCATED BUILD BUDGET FROM A PHANTOM 33/33/33. Treating the criteria as equally weighted invites splitting engineering effort into equal thirds and optimizing for a known scoring function. Because no weighting is published, judges may in practice weight Functionality far above the others — the Functionality blurb is the only one written as a hard pass/fail gate ("Someone with zero Agent Studio knowledge should be able to get through it without hitting a dead end"), while Data Quality and Agent Diversity read as graded depth. A submission that hits 100% on data richness but has one dead end in the activation flow could fail on the criterion that actually gates, having spent a third of its budget on a criterion assumed to be worth exactly as much. The safe posture is to treat Functionality as a gate to clear absolutely, then maximize the other two — not to trade them off against each other at parity.

2. UNDER-RESERVING FOR PHASE 2. This is the larger risk and it compounds the first. The researcher correctly flagged that phase 2 adds undisclosed criteria, but pairing that with a false "explicit" rubric creates a dangerous confidence: a team that believes the published rubric is fully specified will spend the entire build window optimizing three known criteria and ship with nothing in reserve. Since the criteria are literally undisclosed, no amount of optimizing the published three de-risks phase 2. AiKi should reserve capacity and keep the architecture flexible — and note that the top-3 shortlist happens before phase 2, so phase 2 is the round that actually decides the $30,000 and the official-adoption prize.

3. A WRONG MODEL OF SCORE AGGREGATION. The dropped "then compared" matters. If an engineer models judging as three independent scores averaged, the rational play is to maximize expected mean and accept variance — a polarizing, opinionated submission that one judge loves and one hates averages out fine. But "then compared" means judges reconcile, and in a comparison round a single judge's strong objection gets voiced and can propagate rather than being silently averaged away. That argues for eliminating obvious objections (the dead end, the neglected fourth category) over chasing a standout feature that only one judge will champion. Note that Agent Diversity is explicitly written as a penalty criterion — "A submission that treats one category as the main event and the rest as an afterthought won't score well here" — so shipping rebalancing beautifully and stubbing grid trading, yield, and health factor is exactly the failure the rubric is built to catch, regardless of weighting.

Bottom line: the researcher's three-criteria structure and the phase-2 warning are safe to build on. The word "explicitly" in front of "equally weighted" must be struck, and no scoring model or effort-allocation plan should assume a 33/33/33 split. Separately, do not let anyone build against an "ERC-8004/ERC-8183 substrate on BSC" until a contract address is produced — the sources contain none.

claim: The TermiX partner track is the only track with published numeric weights: 30/30/20/20 (Value of services 30%; Proven agent advantage 30%; High-stakes categories & track record 20%; Marketplace quality 20%), with an "Agent Advantage Report" deliverable worth $6,000 for first place, largely orthogonal to the main-track build.
reasoning:
I tried hard to break this and could not break the numeric core. It survives.

CONFIRMED (verbatim from the cited page, reproduced consistently across four separate fetches):
- TermiX rubric table is exactly "Value of the services 30% / Proven agent advantage 30% / High-stakes categories & track record 20% / Marketplace quality 20%". Sums to 100. Correct.
- TermiX is genuinely the ONLY track carrying numeric weights. I checked every other track specifically: the main track ("Build the BNB Agent Studio Marketplace") lists Functionality, Data Quality, Agent Diversity with NO percentages; Altana and PancakeSwap have NO percentages. The full track list is exhaustively four: Main, Altana, TermiX, PancakeSwap — no fifth track hiding a rubric. I also chased the obvious way this could be wrong: BNB Chain's separate "Ultimate Guide to How We Evaluate Hackathons" could have published a general weighted rubric that back-fills the main track. It does not — five qualitative pillars, explicitly no numeric weights. So the exclusivity claim is not just unrefuted, it is doubly confirmed.
- $6,000 first place is correct: TermiX splits $10,000 as 1st $6,000 / 2nd $3,000 / 3rd $1,000. This reconciles with the blog's "TermiX $10,000 USDT" figure. No invented number.
- The three Agent Advantage Report bullets are substantively accurate.

WHERE IT IS WRONG — one material error and two wording drifts:

1. MATERIAL: "largely orthogonal to the main-track build" is REFUTED by the rubric they themselves quoted. 50% of the TermiX score is the main-track build: "Marketplace quality 20% — find, compare, hire, without instructions" is precisely the main track's Functionality criterion, and "Value of the services 30% — real working agents at a price and speed that beat the alternative" judges the agents surfaced in that same marketplace. The page's own framing is "does hiring an agent ON THIS MARKETPLACE beat doing the job yourself" — TermiX judges the marketplace you built for the main track, not a separate artifact. Only the remaining 50% (Proven agent advantage 30%, High-stakes categories 20%) is incremental work. TermiX is a scoring overlay on the main build plus an evidence report, the opposite of orthogonal.

2. The "overarching question" was presented as verbatim but is a paraphrase. Actual text: "What TermiX is judging, in one line: does hiring an agent on this marketplace actually beat doing the job yourself, and can you prove it with numbers?" — not "outperform manual alternatives, supported by data."

3. The deliverable bullet says "trading, stock or security" — it does NOT include "equities." The word "equities" appears only in the criteria row ("stock/equities agents weighted above general-purpose"). Minor, but the researcher widened the qualifying set. Also, "actual outputs attached" is a clause inside bullet 2, not a fourth standalone bullet — the report has three requirements, not four.

Note on scope: the topic header references a "live ERC-8004/ERC-8183 substrate on BSC." Nothing in this claim touches it and I did not verify it here — it should be checked separately, as those are exactly the kind of standard/version numbers most likely to be fabricated.
corrected_claim: TermiX is correctly the only track with published numeric weights, and 30/30/20/20 plus the $6,000 first prize are accurate as stated. The correction is to the framing: the TermiX track is NOT largely orthogonal to the main-track build — 50% of its rubric (Marketplace quality 20% + Value of the services 30%) scores the same marketplace the main track scores, and TermiX explicitly judges "an agent on this marketplace." The genuinely incremental work is the other 50%: the Agent Advantage Report (3 real tasks run with-agent vs. without, reporting time/cost/output quality with actual outputs attached, at least one task from trading, stock or security) and demonstrated depth in high-stakes categories. Treat TermiX as a scoring overlay on the main build plus an evidence artifact, not a side project.
engineering_impact:
The numbers are safe to build against — an engineer optimizing to 30/30/20/20 and budgeting for the $6,000 first prize will not be misled, and the "only track with weights" conclusion is sound, meaning TermiX is correctly identified as the single place where AiKi can reverse-engineer scoring rather than guess.

The damage comes entirely from the "orthogonal" framing. If AiKi's team believes TermiX is a separable side quest, two concrete failures follow:

1. SEQUENCING FAILURE. "Orthogonal" invites deferring TermiX to the end as a bolt-on write-up. But the report requires 3 real tasks executed THROUGH the marketplace with real time/cost/quality telemetry and actual outputs attached. That is only possible if the marketplace is feature-complete and instrumented well before the 9 September deadline. A team that defers this discovers in the final days that it has no way to produce the evidence, because the hire-execute-log path was never built. The instrumentation — per-task timing, cost accounting, output capture and persistence — is a main-build requirement that must be designed in from the start, not appended.

2. MISALLOCATED EFFORT. Believing the tracks are independent, a team would build the main marketplace and then separately chase TermiX points. In reality 50% of TermiX is already won by main-track work, so the correct strategy is the inverse: build one marketplace well, then add only the measurement harness and deliberately stock trading/stock/security agents (weighted above general-purpose). Treating them as two workstreams duplicates effort and, worse, risks a team optimizing the marketplace for the main track's qualitative criteria while neglecting the "find, compare, hire, without instructions" no-instructions usability bar that TermiX scores explicitly.

Secondary, smaller risk: the widened "trading, stock, security, OR equities" phrasing could lead someone to submit an equities-only task believing it qualifies under a fourth named category. The deliverable text names three. This is likely fine in practice since the criteria row pairs "stock/equities," but it is the kind of drift that should not be relied on when a mandatory qualifying task is at stake.

claim: Submission is a Google Form requiring a GitHub repo link and a payout wallet. There is no DoraHacks page, no demo video requirement, and no public leaderboard or submission list.
reasoning:
I fetched the cited form directly and it says what they claimed. The live Google Form ("Build the Era Hackathon Registration", header: "Join BNB Chain's Agent Studio hackathon to build the top onchain AI agent marketplace for all of our agents") does contain a required "Project GitHub Repo Link" and a required wallet address field, and does NOT contain a demo video, deployed-URL, or license field. The field inventory is accurate except for one omission: the researcher's list leaves out "Teammate Names, Emails, and Roles" (required for teams). I also confirmed via the official hackathon page that the same URL (https://forms.gle/9g9XPNFwnYaHAz9L8) backs BOTH the "Apply as Hacker" and "Submit Project" buttons, so their assertion that the form is the submission vehicle — not merely a registration form, despite its title — is correct. The DoraHacks negative and the no-leaderboard negative also survive: neither the BNB Chain blog post nor the official hackathon page links to DoraHacks, and neither displays a submission list or leaderboard.

WHERE IT BREAKS: the claim is framed as an exhaustive account of submission mechanics ("no deployed-URL field, no license field", "no demo video requirement"), inferring the requirements FROM the form's fields. That inference is invalid. The researcher never fetched https://www.bnbchain.org/en/hackathons/smart-money-era — the page the BNB Chain blog explicitly designates as where "the full scoring rubric, reference agents, and submission requirements will be available." That page carries binding requirements the form has no field for:
- Verbatim: "Your submission must be functional and publicly accessible during judging." This is a hard live-deployment obligation. The absence of a deployed-URL form field does NOT mean there is no deployed-URL requirement — it means the requirement is enforced off-form, across the Sep 9–23 judging window.
- Main track: functional publicly accessible marketplace, must support all four agent categories equally, agents must be live on BSC.
- TermiX Challenge (mandatory): an "Agent Advantage Report" with "At least 3 real tasks run both ways", reporting time, cost, and output quality WITH ATTACHMENTS, and "At least one task must come from trading, stock or security."
- Altana track: live onchain transactions visible in the Altana explorer, agents on their own Altana wallets, real session limits with expiry, sessions registered in Keystore, user-facing revocation controls.
- Published rubrics exist: main track = Functionality / Data Quality / Agent Diversity (no percentage weights published); TermiX = value of services 30%, proven agent advantage 30%, high-stakes categories & track record 20%, marketplace quality 20%. Judging is two-phase, with more criteria assessed in phase 2.

So "no demo video requirement" is narrowly true (I found no video requirement on either primary source), but the surrounding claim understates the deliverables by a wide margin. Separately, on the topic header's "live ERC-8004/ERC-8183 substrate": NO ERC-8004 or ERC-8183 contract addresses on BSC appear on any page I fetched. ERC-8004 (identity/reputation/validation registries) and ERC-8183 (agent-to-agent commerce, via the BNBAgent SDK) are real and BNB-Chain-announced, but any specific BSC address must be treated as unverified until read from bnb-chain/bnbagent-sdk or erc-8004/erc-8004-contracts directly.
corrected_claim: Submission and registration share one Google Form (https://forms.gle/9g9XPNFwnYaHAz9L8, titled "Build the Era Hackathon Registration"), which requires a GitHub repo link, a wallet address, and — for teams — teammate names/emails/roles. There is no DoraHacks page, no demo video requirement, and no public leaderboard or submission list. HOWEVER, the form is not the full submission spec. The official page at https://www.bnbchain.org/en/hackathons/smart-money-era imposes requirements with no corresponding form field, most critically: "Your submission must be functional and publicly accessible during judging" (Sep 9–23), all four agent categories supported equally, agents live on BSC, plus a mandatory TermiX "Agent Advantage Report" (3+ real tasks run both ways, with attachments, at least one from trading/stock/security) and Altana-track session/Keystore/revocation requirements. Published rubrics: main track = Functionality / Data Quality / Agent Diversity (weights unpublished); TermiX = 30/30/20/20. Judging is two-phase. No ERC-8004/ERC-8183 BSC contract addresses are published on any of these pages.
engineering_impact: The dangerous inference is "the form asks only for a repo link, therefore a repo is the deliverable." An AiKi engineer building on that version would treat the GitHub repo as the artifact and skip hosting — and get eliminated at the gate, because the marketplace must be functional and publicly accessible for the entire Sep 9–23 judging window. That means AiKi needs paid, monitored, uptime-guaranteed infrastructure standing for two weeks AFTER the Sep 9 build cutoff, a cost and on-call burden that has to be budgeted now, not discovered in September. Second, the rubric is Functionality / Data Quality / Agent Diversity against LIVE agents on BSC — so an AiKi marketplace demoing mocked or seeded agent data scores near zero on two of three criteria; it must index real ERC-8004 registry state on BSC. Third, "support all four agent categories equally" is a hard scope constraint: an AiKi build that specializes in one vertical (e.g. only trading agents) is structurally disqualified from the main track no matter how polished. Fourth, forfeiting the $10k TermiX sub-prize by omission — the Agent Advantage Report is a mandatory benchmarking artifact requiring 3+ real tasks executed both with and without agents, with timing/cost/quality attachments; that is days of experimental work with no form field to remind you it exists, so it will simply not get done if you plan from the form. Finally, if anyone hardcodes an ERC-8004 or ERC-8183 registry address from memory rather than reading it from bnb-chain/bnbagent-sdk, AiKi's indexer silently reads an empty or wrong registry and the "Data Quality" score collapses.

claim: The build window has an exact UTC deadline stated only in the registration form, not in the blog or hackathon page. Supporting detail: the form's availability-confirmation field reads build period "12:00pm UTC+0, Aug 5 2026 – 12:00pm UTC+0, Sep 9 2026"; hard cutoff is therefore 12:00 UTC on 9 Sep 2026.
reasoning:
I fetched all three cited pages, including raw HTML (curl) rather than relying on rendered/summarized text.

WHAT IS CONFIRMED — the deadline value itself.
1) Google Form (https://docs.google.com/forms/d/e/1FAIpQLSdFb30r24sZcFJVDbMqXNJ1_45BJHanc7eFqwUniScDYZfX9A/viewform), form-description block and og:description meta, verbatim: "Join BNB Chain's Agent Studio hackathon to build the top onchain AI agent marketplace for all of our agents. Build period 12:00pm UTC+0, Aug 5 2026 - 12:00pm UTC+0, Sep 9 2026. Judging Sep 9, 2026 - Sep 23, 2026." (form title: "Build the Era Hackathon Registration"; Telegram link https://t.me/+MhiOLT0YUnlmNWFk).
2) forms.gle/9g9XPNFwnYaHAz9L8 (the link the hackathon page itself uses for both "apply as hacker" and "submit project") 302-redirects to exactly that form ID, so it is the canonical registration/submission form.
So "12:00 UTC on 9 Sep 2026, a midday not midnight cutoff" is CORRECT.

WHAT IS REFUTED — two things.

(a) "Stated ONLY in the registration form, not in the ... hackathon page." False. The hackathon landing page's own embedded CMS payload carries the same machine-readable timestamps, verbatim from the page source at https://www.bnbchain.org/en/hackathons/smart-money-era:
  "apply_as_hacker_end_time":"2026-09-09T12:00:00", "apply_as_hacker_start_time":"2026-08-05T12:00:00",
  "start":"2026-08-05T12:00:00", "end":"2026-09-09T12:00:00",
  "submit_project_start_time":"2026-08-05T12:00:00", "submit_project_end_time":"2026-09-09T12:00:00",
  "timezone":"UTC +0", "status":"Ongoing", "slug":"smart-money-era", "id":20020, "date_updated":"2026-08-05T10:11:42.000Z".
Only the *rendered* text is coarse ("5 Aug - 9 Sep, 2026 (UTC +0)" under the "Time" label). The precise 12:00 UTC+0 boundary is present on the hackathon page, and the hackathon CMS is plainly the upstream source that the form description was written from — the form is the copy, not the sole record.

(b) The quote is misattributed to the wrong form field. The availability-confirmation question reads, verbatim and in full: "Please confirm your availability for the build period (Aug 5 - Sep 9) and judging dates (Sep 9 - Sep 23)?" with the single radio option "Yes, I confirm availability". It contains NO times and NO timezone. The "12:00pm UTC+0" string lives in the form's header/description blurb, several fields earlier. A researcher who cited the availability field as the source of the UTC timestamp did not read the form's DOM.

Also verified about the blog (https://www.bnbchain.org/en/blog/build-the-era-build-the-official-bnb-agent-studio-marketplace, datePublished 2026-08-05T11:54:26+00:00): the claim that it is timezone-less and year-less is CORRECT. Zero occurrences of "UTC", "GMT", "12:00", or "23:59" in the raw HTML; Key Dates reads exactly "Build period: Aug 5 - Sep 9", "Judging: Sep 9 - Sep 23", "Winner announcement: Nov 5". Note additionally that "Nov 5" appears ONLY in the blog — it is absent from the hackathon page and from the form, so the winner-announcement date is single-sourced and should not be treated as firm.

Two further caveats the original claim glosses over: "12:00pm" is an inherently ambiguous notation (it means noon here, corroborated by the CMS "T12:00:00", but the two representations agreeing is what makes it safe, not the form alone); and the CMS timestamps are naive datetimes whose zone comes from a separate "timezone":"UTC +0" field — so the pairing, not the timestamp, is what pins the zone.
corrected_claim: The build window's exact cutoff is 12:00 UTC on 9 Sep 2026 (a midday deadline, 2026-09-09T12:00:00Z), and that precision appears in at least TWO places, not only the registration form: (1) the Google Form's description header — "Build period 12:00pm UTC+0, Aug 5 2026 - 12:00pm UTC+0, Sep 9 2026" — which is the form's blurb, NOT its availability-confirmation field; and (2) the hackathon landing page's embedded CMS record, which carries "submit_project_end_time":"2026-09-09T12:00:00" / "end":"2026-09-09T12:00:00" alongside "timezone":"UTC +0". Judging (Sep 9-23) also has no stated time of day anywhere, so AiKi's public deployment and BSC-live agents must stay up through the whole of 23 Sep local-generous, not until some assumed hour — the hackathon page requires the submission be "functional and publicly accessible during judging" and that agents be "live on BSC," so an infra teardown or expiring RPC key/cert mid-window is the realer failure mode than the deadline itself.

claim: The four-category framing is accurate per the BNB Chain "Smart Money Era" hackathon page (Rebalancing / Grid Trading / Yield Optimisation / Health Factor Monitoring), but the blog uses a different first category — "Monitoring" instead of "Rebalancing". The hackathon page is the operative rules surface and its four categories are the ones named in the Agent Diversity criterion; build to the hackathon page, and consider surfacing generic monitoring as a fifth facet to cover the blog framing.
reasoning:
I tried to break this and could not. I pulled both cited URLs as raw HTML via curl (HTTP 200, 504KB and 389KB) rather than relying on a summarizing fetcher, and grepped for each quoted string. Every quotation the researcher gave is verbatim-exact.

HACKATHON PAGE — the table is present under "What You're Building", introduced by "Four categories, all first-class:" with header "| Category | What the agent does |". Rows exactly as quoted: "**Rebalancing** | Manages LP ranges, resets positions automatically", "**Grid Trading** | Places and manages automated grid orders", "**Yield Optimisation** | Routes liquidity to the highest available APR", "**Health Factor Monitoring** | Protects lending positions from liquidation". Immediately after: "Single-category submissions score poorly. All four, equally deep, is the bar."

AGENT DIVERSITY CRITERION — confirmed verbatim, and it is decisive for the researcher's argument because it re-lists the hackathon page's own four terms: "All four categories (rebalancing, grid trading, yield, health factor) surfaced with equal depth. A submission that treats one category as the main event and the rest as an afterthought won't score well here." Note it says "rebalancing", not "monitoring". Rubric is three criteria scored by three judges independently: Functionality, Data Quality, Agent Diversity.

BLOG PAGE — confirmed verbatim under "Ideas for What to List": "...we'll share reference agents and skills from our partners to build against, spanning four categories:" followed by "Monitoring agents: watching markets, wallets, and positions", "Grid trading agents: running automated strategies within set ranges", "Health factor agents: tracking loan positions and acting before liquidation", "Yield agents: moving capital to where it earns most". The word "rebalanc" does not appear anywhere in the blog HTML (zero grep hits).

PRESS RELEASE — the researcher cited no URL for it, so I treated it as unsupported and searched independently. A Chainwire release dated 2026-08-05 (syndicated to Benzinga, TradingView, CryptoPotato, KuCoin) carries the same monitoring/grid/health-factor/yield list. Their "and press release" holds up.

TWO REFINEMENTS, neither fatal:

(1) "the blog uses a different first category — Monitoring instead of Rebalancing" understates the delta. It is not a positional rename. The two lists are in different orders entirely (blog: Monitoring, Grid, Health factor, Yield; hackathon: Rebalancing, Grid, Yield, Health Factor Monitoring). The substantive fact is that the blog OMITS Rebalancing — the hardest category, since LP range management is the only one requiring concentrated-liquidity position math — and promotes generic monitoring into its slot, while also splitting "monitoring" away from what the hackathon page bundles as "Health Factor Monitoring".

(2) The advisory tail is the weakest part and is mildly counterproductive. The blog explicitly disqualifies itself as a rules surface, in a sentence the researcher did not quote: "Treat these as guidance, not a definitive list or judging criteria. They're there to show the range a marketplace should be able to handle; if yours supports these four well, it can handle what comes next." So there is no blog framing that needs "covering". Meanwhile the hackathon page demands "All four, equally deep" and Agent Diversity penalizes uneven depth. Splitting finite build effort across five buckets to satisfy a source that disclaims itself trades depth for breadth against the one criterion that measures depth.

Adjacent spot-check, since the topic names it: ERC-8004 appears 34x on the hackathon page and 8x on the blog ("the standard for onchain agent identity", ~200,000 agents registered on BSC). ERC-8183 appears 14x on the hackathon page but ZERO times on the blog, and only inside the Altana partner track — "ERC-8183 buyer side, hireErc8183Agent", "Altana ERC-8183 SDK" at docs.altana.network/sdk/erc8183. It is a partner-track bonus, not a main-track requirement. No contract addresses are published on either page.
corrected_claim: The verbatim category tables and the Agent Diversity wording are exactly as stated — build the four hackathon-page categories (Rebalancing, Grid Trading, Yield Optimisation, Health Factor Monitoring) and treat those as canonical, since Agent Diversity names those four terms including "rebalancing". Two corrections to the framing: the blog does not rename Rebalancing to Monitoring, it drops Rebalancing entirely and adds a generic monitoring bucket; and no fifth facet is warranted, because the blog itself states "Treat these as guidance, not a definitive list or judging criteria", while the hackathon page states "Single-category submissions score poorly. All four, equally deep, is the bar." Generic monitoring should be implemented as cross-cutting UI surfacing (live position/market state shown within each of the four categories), not as a fifth top-level category competing for depth.
engineering_impact:
Two distinct failure modes for AiKi. First, if an engineer built to the blog list instead of the hackathon page, AiKi would ship no Rebalancing category at all — and Rebalancing is explicitly enumerated in the Agent Diversity criterion. That is a direct scoring hit on one of only three rubric criteria, judged independently by three judges, and it removes the single most technically demanding integration (concentrated-liquidity LP range management, i.e. the PancakeSwap v3 surface). Discovering that late is expensive because LP range logic is not a UI relabel.

Second, if an engineer acted on the researcher's fifth-facet advice, AiKi would build five top-level category surfaces where the rubric rewards four at equal depth. Every hour spent on a generic Monitoring bucket is an hour not spent deepening Rebalancing or Health Factor, against a criterion whose stated failure mode is exactly uneven depth. The category taxonomy is also load-bearing for schema: agent-type enums, filter/facet routes, and any indexer partitioning key. A five-value enum shipped now means a migration plus dead routes later, and a marketplace whose navigation does not match the four category names judges will be looking for.

Third-order: do not gate main-track work on ERC-8183. It appears only in the Altana partner track as a bonus, is absent from the blog, and there are no published contract addresses on either page — so any main-track dependency on hireErc8183Agent would be building core flow on an optional, partner-scoped surface.

reasoning:
I tried to break this and could not. Both sources were fetched independently (raw HTTP 200, full text extracted, not just via a summarizing fetcher).

1) PRESS RELEASE — verbatim quote is exact. The Chainwire release (dated 05 Aug 2026, "Dubai, UAE, August 5th, 2026, Chainwire") contains, word for word: "Submissions will be scored against published criteria covering functionality, data quality, agent diversity, and real-world usage, with full details available when the build period opens. Partner tracks, where applicable, are judged separately according to each sponsor's own criteria." The quote the researcher gave is accurate down to the punctuation. Syndicated copies (Benzinga, CryptoPotato, TradingView, MEXC) carry the identical sentence, so it is not a Chainwire-only rendering artifact.

2) HACKATHON PAGE — only three criteria, confirmed by string search, not by eyeballing a summary. The "How You're Judged" section reads: "Three judges, scored independently, then compared," followed by a table with headers "Criterion | Weight" and exactly three rows — Functionality, Data Quality, Agent Diversity — each with descriptive text and, notably, an EMPTY Weight cell (no percentages are published). The word "usage" appears ZERO times anywhere in the 504KB of page HTML (including the partner-track and eligibility sections and the RSC payload); "real-world" appears zero times; the only "real world" hits are the site-wide nav item "Real World Assets." I also enumerated every external link on the page — there is no linked rules doc, Notion, or PDF that could hold a fuller rubric. So the fourth criterion genuinely is absent from where entrants will look.

3) THE PHASE-2 GAP IS REAL AND ACKNOWLEDGED. Immediately after the three-row table the page says, verbatim (typos theirs): "We'all also assess more criterias in the second phase, stay tuned to find out!" and the Timeline lists "Phase 2 : [REDACTED]". So BNB Chain explicitly admits undisclosed additional criteria exist. This corroborates the researcher's framing.

WHAT I WOULD TRIM AS OVERSTATEMENT (the only soft spot): the researcher's line "This is the most likely content of the undisclosed 'Phase 2' criteria" is inference, not sourced. Nothing on either page ties "real-world usage" to Phase 2. Two readings are equally live: (a) it is a Phase-2 criterion, or (b) the PR simply over-described a rubric that shipped with three criteria — note the PR promised "full details available when the build period opens," the build period opened the same day (Aug 5), and the published details show three criteria with blank weights, which is a straightforward PR-vs-page inconsistency. Also unsourced is the operational definition: neither document defines "real-world usage," so "unique wallets, activations, completed hires" is the researcher's own gloss, not BNB Chain's. A cheaper, equally plausible reading is the page's actual hard eligibility rule — "Agents surfaced on your marketplace must be live on BSC" and "Your submission must be functional and publicly accessible during judging" — i.e. real agents doing real transactions rather than a usage-metrics leaderboard.

Verdict: the factual claim is CONFIRMED; the causal attribution to Phase 2 and the metric definition are the parts to hedge.
corrected_claim: CONFIRMED as stated, with one hedge. Accurate version: the Chainwire release names four scoring areas — "functionality, data quality, agent diversity, and real-world usage" — while the bnbchain.org/en/hackathons/smart-money-era page publishes a three-row "How You're Judged" table (Functionality, Data Quality, Agent Diversity) with a Weight column that is left blank, and the word "usage" appears nowhere on the page. The page separately admits "We'all also assess more criterias in the second phase" with Phase 2 marked "[REDACTED]". However, no source connects "real-world usage" to Phase 2 — that is inference, and it is equally consistent with the PR having over-described a rubric that shipped with three criteria. Neither source defines what "real-world usage" would measure, so treat "unique wallets / activations / completed hires" as an unverified guess rather than a known metric.
engineering_impact:
The claim is true, so building on it is safe — but building on the *gloss* is where AiKi gets hurt.

If an engineer treats "real-world usage = unique wallets, activations, completed hires" as a known, scored metric, the failure mode is misallocated effort in a 5-week build (Aug 5 – Sep 9, judging Sep 9 – Sep 23): shipping an analytics/telemetry subsystem — event pipeline, wallet dedup, funnel dashboards — against a criterion whose definition is unpublished and whose weight is literally blank on the rubric, while the three criteria that ARE published are all about the hire journey. The page states the primary bar plainly: judged on "how easily someone can discover and hire an agent," "someone with zero Agent Studio knowledge should be able to get through it without hitting a dead end," and Agent Diversity is a scoring trap — "Single-category submissions score poorly. All four, equally deep, is the bar." Time taken from equal-depth coverage of all four categories (rebalancing, grid trading, yield, health factor) to build usage dashboards is a direct scoring loss on a criterion that is confirmed and published.

The second failure mode is inverted: if a future PR/marketing doc were treated as authoritative over the hackathon page, AiKi could also *skip* things that are hard eligibility gates. Those are on the page and are binary, not scored — "Agents surfaced on your marketplace must be live on BSC" and "Your submission must be functional and publicly accessible during judging" (plus the Altana partner track requiring live testnet/mainnet transactions). Missing those disqualifies regardless of rubric interpretation.

Correct engineering posture: keep the researcher's recommendation but downgrade its cost. Emit usage events (activation, hire-completed, wallet-first-seen) as cheap append-only telemetry from day one — that is a few hours of work and hedges the Phase-2 unknown — but do NOT build a metrics product, and do not let it compete with end-to-end journey polish and equal-depth coverage of all four agent categories. Also plan for a Phase 2 whose criteria are genuinely unknown ("[REDACTED]"): keep the deployment live and instrumented past the Sep 9 submission close through the Nov 5 winner announcement, since the top 3 are shortlisted publicly and then re-assessed.

claim: Required integrations: ERC-8004 agent identity and BSC are required; BNB Agent Studio itself is not stated as a mandatory build dependency for the marketplace front end.
reasoning:
I pulled both cited pages as raw HTML (HTTP 200, 504KB and 388KB) and extracted every occurrence of "8004", "8183", "x402", "Agent Studio", "Keystore", so the finding is based on full-page text, not a summarizer's paraphrase. Note: an initial WebFetch summary of the hackathon page invented a "Mandatory Integrations" section listing the BNB Agent Studio CLI and the ERC-8183 SDK. That section does not exist in the page. I discarded it.

PART 2 (BSC) — CONFIRMED. The hackathon page's Eligibility block is the only hard-requirement list for the main track, and it has exactly four bullets: open globally; one entry per team; "Your submission must be functional and publicly accessible during judging."; "Agents surfaced on your marketplace must be live on BSC." Verbatim match.

PART 3 (Agent Studio not a mandatory build dependency) — CONFIRMED, and better supported than the researcher argued. Agent Studio appears in three roles, none of them a dependency: (a) the prize — "official adoption as the BNB Agent Studio marketplace, the canonical front door for every agent on BSC"; (b) a Tooling/Resources note about shipping agents, not the marketplace — "Describe it, and Cursor scaffolds it against the BNB Agent Studio CLI... Agent Studio runs on AWS underneath; that's just how it works, not a separate track to build for"; (c) a rubric phrase that cuts against dependency — "Someone with zero Agent Studio knowledge should be able to get through it without hitting a dead end."

PART 1 (ERC-8004 required) — NOT SUPPORTED. ERC-8004 is never stated as a requirement on either page. On the hackathon page every one of the 34 "8004" hits sits inside one block: the Resources section for 8004scan (by AltLayer), a third-party discovery tool offering free Pro-tier API access. It is absent from Eligibility and absent from all three rubric criteria (Functionality, Data Quality, Agent Diversity). On the blog it appears only as market context ("More than 200,000 AI agents are registered on BNB Smart Chain under ERC-8004, the standard for onchain agent identity") and as an affordance, explicitly framed as a head start rather than a mandate: "You're not starting from zero. Agents registered under ERC-8004 already carry an onchain identity and a track record other software can look up; your job is to make that legible." Elevating this to sit alongside BSC — which IS in the enumerated Eligibility list — is a category error between a stated rule and a supplied resource.

ALSO WRONG IN THE SUPPORTING DETAIL:
1. The quoted main-track mandate is fabricated as a quote. They wrote: "a front-end marketplace where users discover, understand, and activate AI agents." The page says: "A front end that surfaces agent data, lets users discover and activate agents by category, and doesn't make them think too hard about it."
2. Material omission — they dropped the single hardest constraint on the front end. The page mandates four first-class categories (Rebalancing, Grid Trading, Yield Optimisation, Health Factor Monitoring) and states: "Single-category submissions score poorly. All four, equally deep, is the bar." This is enforced by the Agent Diversity rubric criterion. Their "required integrations" framing omits it entirely.
3. Source conflict they did not catch: the blog lists a DIFFERENT four ("Monitoring agents, Grid trading agents, Health factor agents, Yield agents") and disclaims them — "Treat these as guidance, not a definitive list or judging criteria" — while the blog also says "The main challenge is open, with no fixed tracks." The hackathon page contradicts both and governs. Blog "Monitoring" is not page "Rebalancing".
4. On x402 and ERC-8183 they are right, and could have been stronger: on the hackathon page both appear ONLY under the Altana track heading "Bonus:" — "Hire BNB Agent Studio agents through ERC-8183 using the Altana ERC-8183 SDK" and "Implement sell over x402/B402 using the x402 server SDK." Neither is required even within the Altana track. So the topic framing of a "live ERC-8004/ERC-8183 substrate" as required substrate is wrong for 8183 too.
5. Altana hard requirements are accurately reported and verbatim-correct (call allowlist, spend cap, expiry; Keystore registration; real onchain txs through a session key; user-facing revocation), but they omitted the gating condition — "your submission must show live onchain transactions in the Altana explorer (testnet or mainnet)" — and the Prizes-tab instruction to "include your wallet address(es) in your submission." TermiX Agent Advantage Report and PancakeSwap real-benefit are confirmed verbatim.
6. Prize figures conflict across the two sources: blog says "$40,000+ in prizes", hackathon page header says "30,000 USD Prize Pool". Both are official; the researcher cited neither.

Timing check: build period 5 Aug – 9 Sep 2026 (UTC+0), judging 9–23 Sep, winner announced 5 Nov. Today is 18 Aug 2026, so roughly 22 days remain.
corrected_claim: Only two things are stated as hard requirements for the main track, both in the Eligibility list: the submission must be functional and publicly accessible during judging, and "Agents surfaced on your marketplace must be live on BSC." ERC-8004 is NOT a stated requirement — it is background context (the identity standard the ~200k BSC agents happen to be registered under) plus a supplied resource (8004scan's free Pro API, page-stated at 500 req/min and 100,000 req/day). BNB Agent Studio is correctly not a build dependency for the front end; it is the adoption prize and an agent-authoring tool, and the page says its AWS backend is "not a separate track to build for." ERC-8183 and x402/B402 are explicitly labelled "Bonus" within the Altana partner track, not requirements anywhere. The binding constraint the claim omits is the four-category mandate — Rebalancing, Grid Trading, Yield Optimisation, Health Factor Monitoring, all equally deep — scored via the Agent Diversity criterion, with the page warning "Single-category submissions score poorly."
engineering_impact:
Two opposite failure modes, both caused by mislabeling a resource as a requirement.

If AiKi treats ERC-8004 as a mandated integration, engineering time goes into on-chain identity/registry plumbing and an 8004-registry-only ingestion path, as if compliance were being scored. It is not scored anywhere. That budget is drawn from the two things that ARE scored — Data Quality and Agent Diversity — and it also silently narrows the catalogue: any BSC-live agent not registered under 8004 gets excluded by an architecture built around a mandate that does not exist, even though the actual rule ("live on BSC") admits it.

If AiKi over-corrects on the true half of this claim and treats 8004 as merely optional, it loses the only practical path to the Data Quality bar, which demands "real-time, accurate data that goes beyond basic counts" sufficient for "a genuinely informed call on which agent to hire." Reputation, feedback, and track-record fields realistically come from the 8004scan API, and its free Pro tier must be applied for via the Developer Hub plus a Google Form — a lead-time dependency that will not resolve on submission day with 22 days left.

The most expensive error is the omission, not the overstatement. Building against the researcher's summary yields a marketplace with no explicit four-category structure, or one deep category plus three thin ones. The page states outright that this scores poorly, and Agent Diversity is a third of the main rubric. Worse, an engineer working from the blog alone would implement a "Monitoring" category; the governing hackathon page requires "Rebalancing." That is a wrong taxonomy baked into the data model, the routing, and the filter UI — the costliest layer to change late.

Finally, if the Altana bounty is in scope, treating ERC-8183/x402 as required inverts the priority: they are Bonus, while the gating condition is live onchain transactions visible in the Altana explorer through a Keystore-registered session key with in-product revocation. Shipping 8183 escrow but no revocation UI disqualifies; shipping revocation with no 8183 still competes.

I fetched both cited pages independently (WebFetch plus raw curl of the HTML and embedded Next.js JSON, so I read the CMS source strings rather than a summarizer's paraphrase). Every enumerated figure checks out verbatim.

CONFIRMED verbatim from the blog: "$40,000+ in prizes from BNB Chain and ecosystem partners on top, plus token and credit rewards"; the Prizes list is exactly "BNB Chain: $30,000 USDT / TermiX: $10,000 USDT / PancakeSwap: 1,000 CAKE / AltLayer: 8004scan Pro plans and AltLLM credits [amounts TBC] / Altana: 50,000 XP"; heading "TermiX: $10,000 USDT Total Prize"; and "Three partner tracks run alongside the main challenge" (TermiX, Altana, PancakeSwap). Winner takes all, awarded to one team."; "1,000 CAKE for the best submission...". No 2nd/3rd line exists anywhere on the main track, so that part of the claim holds by absence. Dates confirmed: 5 Aug - 9 Sep 2026.

WHERE THE CLAIM BREAKS DOWN - three things:

1. The "denomination not contractually pinned" inference is unsupported and contradicted by the researcher's own primary source. They built an argument on the word "equivalent" while ignoring that the same organiser's blog states flatly "BNB Chain: $30,000 USDT". The two BNB Chain pages differ in specificity; "equivalent" on one page is not evidence that the settlement asset is unpinned, and the blog is the more specific statement. This is an invented financial/legal conclusion, not a sourced fact.

2. "Advertised as $40,000+" is true of the blog only. The hackathon page's own structured field is "prize_pool":30000 and the on-page widget renders "Prize Pool: 30,000 USD". The claim presents one consistent headline where the two cited pages actually disagree by $10k+. The $40,000+ figure is internally coherent (30k + 10k USDT = 40k, with CAKE/XP/credits as the "+"), but the hackathon page does not advertise it.

3. "Unspecified AltLayer credits" as a prize-structure line item is the weakest part. There is no AltLayer track, no AltLayer bounty, and no AltLayer entry in the hackathon page's Prizes & Bounties section at all — AltLayer appears only as a sponsor logo and under Resources, where the actual offer reads: "Free Pro-tier access for hackathon participants: eligible participants receive complimentary access to the 8004scan Pro API tier for the duration of the hackathon. Up to 500 API requests per minute / Up to 100,000 requests per day", applied for via the 8004scan Developer Hub plus a Google Form. That is participation tooling open to everyone who applies, not a competitive award to a winner. "AltLLM credits" appears only in the blog list, marked "[amounts TBC]", with zero corresponding detail on the hackathon page.

Two material caveats the claim silently dropped: Altana's 50,000 XP carries "(Allocation mechanics to be confirmed.)", and TermiX eligibility is gated — "Submissions must include the required Agent Advantage Report to be eligible" (a comparison of at least three real tasks run with and without an agent). The "56:0x8004...:269666" form is 8004scan's proprietary composite primary key — it omits the eip155 namespace and overloads the name agent_id — and should be treated as an indexer artifact, not a protocol identifier.
engineering_impact:
The address half is safe to build on, so nothing breaks there — but AiKi should read it from the bnbagent-sdk network preset (or ERC8004_REGISTRY_ADDRESS) rather than hardcoding, because the mainnet/testnet addresses genuinely differ. An engineer who internalizes "ERC-8004 is the same address on every chain" and hardcodes 0x8004A169... will point testnet writes at a nonexistent contract on chain 97 and get silent reverts or empty reads in staging.

The ID half is where real damage happens. If AiKi adopts "56:0x8004...:269666" as its canonical agent identifier:

1. On-chain calls break immediately. IdentityRegistry is an ERC-721 whose functions (ownerOf, tokenURI, transfers, and the 8004 write intents the SDK exposes) take a bare uint256 tokenId. Any code path that passes the composite string through to a contract call must string-split it first; if that parsing lives in one place and is forgotten in another, AiKi gets a class of bugs where reads work (indexer) but writes fail (chain).

2. Interop with the wider 8004 ecosystem silently fails to resolve. A2A AgentCards and other ERC-8004 tooling exchange the spec pair (agentRegistry with the eip155: prefix, plus a numeric agentId). AiKi emitting or matching on a de-namespaced 56:... string will fail to join against any counterparty's records — and it fails as a lookup miss, not an exception, so trust/reputation resolution just quietly returns nothing. That is the worst failure mode for a marketplace: agents appear unrated rather than erroring.

3. Indexer lock-in at the schema layer. Storing 8004scan's composite as a DB primary key bakes a third-party format into AiKi's data model. If 8004scan changes the format, rate-limits, or AiKi switches to reading the chain directly or to another indexer, every stored key needs migration. The durable key is (chain_id, registry_address, token_id) as separate columns, rendered to the eip155-prefixed spec form at the API boundary.

Net: trust the address, reject the ID format, and store identity decomposed rather than as an indexer string.
